title: Unveiling the antiviral inhibitory activity of ebselen and ebsulfur derivatives on SARS-CoV-2 using machine learning-bas

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines pIC₅₀ = (1 / IC₅₀ (M)). The correct conversion is pIC₅₀ = −log₁₀(IC₅₀ in M) (i.e., log₁₀(1/IC₅₀)). The stated formula is dimensionally and numerically wrong and would produce values completely different from the pIC₅₀ values used throughout (e.g., 0.05–8 range).

Abstract states 'the R² values of MLR, RF, and ANN models for the training set were 0.83, 0.82, and 0.92', but Results report 'R² of the training set = 0.69' for MLR and 'R² of 0.89 for the training set' for ANN (the Conclusion also restates 0.89 for ANN). Two of the three abstract R² values contradict the body.

Abstract reports test RMSE of 0.27 (MLR), 0.18 (RF), and 0.09 (ANN), while the Results report 'RMSE of the test set = 0.56' for MLR and 'RMSE of 0.05 for the test set' for ANN (the Conclusion repeats 0.05). The MLR and ANN test errors are inconsistent between abstract and body.

The text states 'Gini importance varies between 0 and 1, with 0 representing the lowest and best possible importance. A higher Gini importance indicates greater.' This is self-contradictory (0 cannot be both the lowest and the best) and contradicts the preceding sentence that the features with the highest Gini importance are the most impactful.

The grid for min_samples_split includes the value 1. In scikit-learn (the stated framework, Grid-Search CV of Scikit-learn), min_samples_split must be ≥ 2 (an integer of 1 raises an error), so this hyperparameter value is impossible as described.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1(a) vs. Methods RF paragraph and Results (best RF model)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Methods state the RF was tuned by varying four parameters: 'Max feature', 'Min_sample_leaf', 'Min_samples_split' and 'number of estimators', and the Results report the best model has 'a max feature of 4'. However, Table 1(a) does not list max_features at all; instead it lists 'Max depth' (8–12), which is not described in the Methods text. The reported optimal setting therefore does not correspond to the tabulated search grid.

Text says 'Hyperparameter optimization for the ANN includes determining the number of hidden layers, the number of neurons, the maximum number of iterations (max_iter), the learning rate, and the batch size' and that 'the five hyperparameters of the ANN model are examined, is presented in Table 1(b)'. Table 1(b) lists only four hyperparameters (hidden layers, neurons, learning rate, batch size); max_iter is absent.

R² is defined as Σ(y_pred − ȳ)²/Σ(y_exp − ȳ)². This 'explained/total variance' ratio equals the coefficient of determination only for ordinary least-squares fits; for nonlinear models (RF, ANN) and for external predictions it is not equivalent to 1 − SSres/SStot and can exceed 1 or misrepresent fit quality. Given that the reported R² values are for RF/ANN, the formula used is inappropriate/incorrect.

predicted_errors.error_location: Antiviral assay section ('Seven ebselen analogs were tested against four strains of SARS-CoV-2 M^Pro')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Methods describe propagation and infection with a single virus isolate, 'SARS-CoV-2 B.1.617.2 (accession number ON381169)', and the results in Fig. 6C are described for one virus. The claim of testing against 'four strains' is unsupported/contradictory. Moreover, strains of 'SARS-CoV-2 M^Pro' is a category error (strains refer to the virus, not the protease); likewise 'experiments with live SARS-CoV-2 Mᵖʳᵒ ... in a BSL-3 facility' conflates the enzyme with live virus.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Results (enzyme-based assay of new analogs)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The most potent compound only reduced M^Pro activity to 64.5% at 100 µM (i.e., ~35% inhibition, implying IC₅₀ > 100 µM), yet the Abstract claims 'compound P8 resulted in a good potential candidate for SARS-CoV-2 M^Pro inhibitory activity' and the Results claim the ANN-predicted pIC₅₀ values 'were all within the range of the data set' (a dataset of potent, sub-/low-micromolar inhibitors). The experimental data contradict the predicted potencies and do not support the claim of successful prospective validation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods: Kennard–Stone description (ref 18), cytotoxicity (ref 36), TCID₅₀ analysis (ref 43)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: References are used inconsistently across unrelated topics: ref 18 is introduced as a SARS-CoV-2/ebselen inhibition study ('also SARS-CoV-2¹⁸⁻²¹') but is cited to support the Kennard–Stone distance metric; ref 36 is cited for the Kennard–Stone algorithm ('Kennard–Stone³⁵,³⁶') and then again for the cytotoxicity protocol ('evaluated according to the previous description³⁶'); ref 43 is cited for ANN construction and later for TCID₅₀/ml virological analysis. At least some of these attributions must be incorrect.

The text states the simulations repeat short MD runs 'from reasonable protein–ligand configurations, focusing on ligand-unbinding states', while the stated purpose and the ranking criterion (snapshots selected by smallest Se–S(C145) distance, starting with the ligand 30 Å away) correspond to sampling the binding (association) pathway. The description of the resampling criterion is internally inconsistent with the simulation objective.

The same paragraph first states 'P8 rearranged its conformation by orienting the Se of the benzoselenazole moiety toward the S of C145' and then claims 'chalcogen-bonding interaction between S atoms in P8 and C145'. P8 is described as a selenium-containing ebselen analog, so the interaction cannot involve 'S atoms in P8'; the two statements contradict each other.

With R²(train)=0.69, RMSE(train)=0.16 and RMSE(test)=0.56 (a 3.5-fold increase in error on the test set), the paper concludes 'the model was predictively accurate and acceptable'. This is unsupported and contradicts the later statement that the MLR test RMSE made it the worst model.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, external validation with ebselen data from Amporndanai et al.
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: An external RMSE of 0.35 (on only three compounds) is described as demonstrating 'good predictive performance', even though the paper rejects the MLR model on the basis of a smaller test RMSE (0.27 as stated in the abstract) and claims the ANN test RMSE is 0.05. The evaluation criterion is applied inconsistently and the conclusion is overstated for n = 3.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, ANN architecture 4-(5-5-5)-1 trained on 21 compounds
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: An ANN with three hidden layers of five neurons each (≈100 trainable weights) is fitted to 21 training compounds and evaluated on 6 test compounds, yet the model is described as showing 'robust and stable performance'. The parameter-to-sample ratio makes the reported R²=0.89/RMSE=0.05 highly susceptible to overfitting, and no cross-validation statistics for the final model are reported to support robustness.

Methods state compounds were prepared at 500 µM and 'twofold serially diluted to 8 concentrations' (covering ~4–500 µM), but Results state 'Cytotoxicity was not observed in P1, P3, P4, P5, P7, and P8 in any tested concentrations to 100 μM; therefore, we concluded that the compounds' cytotoxicity was higher than 100 μM'. The reported tested range and the concluded CC₅₀ limit are inconsistent with the described dilution scheme.
